sections.name: General Knowledge / Current Affairs of India and Goa

p1.title: Passage 1
paras: When the sea begins to eat into a coast, the instinctive response is to build a wall. Concrete and boulders are piled along the shore, and for a time the houses behind them are safe. But a beach is not a fixed object; it is a moving body of sand, constantly carried away by storms and returned by gentler waves. A wall interrupts this exchange. Waves that once spent their energy running up a sloping beach now strike a vertical face and rebound, scouring the sand in front of the wall and often worsening erosion on the unprotected shore beyond its end. Within a few decades the beach the wall was meant to save may have vanished, leaving the wall standing in deep water and in need of ever more costly repair.

Coastal engineers have therefore grown cautious about hard defences, except where valuable structures leave no alternative. They increasingly favour approaches that work with natural processes: replenishing beaches with sand, protecting the dunes and vegetation that hold it in place, and, most difficult of all, keeping new construction back from the shifting line of the sea. Such measures demand patience and restraint from communities that want visible protection at once. Their merit is that they treat the coast as a system to be managed rather than an enemy to be fought.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: For generations the mangrove forests that fringe tropical coasts were regarded as wasteland: muddy, mosquito-ridden and of no obvious use except as a source of firewood. Their clearance for ports, prawn farms and seaside construction was seen as improvement. Only in recent decades has a fuller accounting begun to emerge. The tangled roots of mangroves trap sediment and slow the force of waves, so that villages behind a healthy belt of mangroves suffer markedly less damage from cyclones and storm surges than those whose shoreline has been cleared. The same roots shelter the young of many fish and crabs, sustaining fisheries far beyond the forest's edge. Mangrove soils, moreover, lock away carbon at rates that exceed those of many inland forests.

Restoration has become fashionable, and planting campaigns now produce impressive photographs of volunteers pressing seedlings into the mud. Results have been mixed. Seedlings planted on mudflats where mangroves never naturally grew, or of a single species chosen for convenience, frequently die within a year. Successful projects tend to be less photogenic: they restore the tidal flow that was blocked by embankments, allow nature to reseed the area, and involve the fishing communities who have the strongest reason to protect the forest once it returns.

questions.q: The main point of the passage is that:
opts: Coastal communities should abandon the shore entirely.
Sea walls are the only reliable protection against storms.
Engineers have found no answer to coastal erosion.
Sea walls often worsen erosion, and working with natural coastal processes is wiser.
questions.why: Main idea: walls interrupt the movement of sand; engineers 'favour approaches that work with natural processes'.

questions.q: According to the passage, when waves strike a vertical wall they:
opts: Deposit extra sand at its base.
Rebound and scour the sand in front of it.
questions.why: Detail: waves 'strike a vertical face and rebound, scouring the sand in front of the wall'.

questions.q: The passage implies that keeping construction back from the sea is "most difficult of all" because it:
opts: Is forbidden by most coastal laws.
Requires communities to give up building close to the shore.
questions.why: Inference: such measures 'demand patience and restraint from communities that want visible protection at once'.

questions.q: The phrase "an enemy to be fought" in the last sentence refers to the attitude behind:
opts: Managing the coast as a system.
Building hard defences such as sea walls.
questions.why: Inference: hard walls confront the sea, whereas the favoured measures 'treat the coast as a system to be managed'.

questions.q: The word "replenishing" most nearly means:
questions.why: Vocabulary: beaches are restored by adding sand back to them.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: Why Inland Forests Store More Carbon
Mangroves: From Wasteland to Coastal Guardian
questions.why: Main idea: mangroves 'were regarded as wasteland', but a 'fuller accounting' shows they protect coasts, fisheries and carbon.

questions.q: Which benefit of mangroves is mentioned in the passage?
opts: They provide fertile soil for growing rice.
They raise water temperature to help prawn farms.
They eliminate mosquitoes from coastal areas.
They reduce the damage that storm surges cause to villages behind them.
questions.why: Detail: villages behind mangroves 'suffer markedly less damage from cyclones and storm surges'.

questions.q: The reference to 'impressive photographs of volunteers' suggests that the author believes:
opts: planting campaigns always succeed within a year.
some restoration efforts value appearance over ecological success.
volunteers should not take part in restoration.
photographs are the best measure of a project's success.
questions.why: Inference: 'Results have been mixed', and 'successful projects tend to be less photogenic', implying visible campaigns are not necessarily effective.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards mangrove restoration is best described as:
opts: uncritically enthusiastic about all planting drives.
supportive of restoration but critical of poorly designed campaigns.
questions.why: Tone: the author praises projects that restore tidal flow and involve fishing communities, while noting that convenient single-species planting 'frequently die within a year'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'photogenic' means:
questions.why: Vocabulary: successful projects are 'less photogenic' than campaigns that 'produce impressive photographs'.

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: “He is married ____ my cousin.”
questions.why: 'Married to' is the fixed form. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to “verbose”:
questions.why: 'Verbose' means using too many words; 'succinct' means briefly expressed. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Identify the error: “She wants to buy an unique gift for her mother’s birthday.”
questions.why: 'Unique' begins with the consonant sound /j/, so 'a unique'. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the correct word: “The red scarf was a perfect ____ to her white dress.”
questions.why: 'Complement' means something that completes; 'compliment' means praise. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the correct passive construction: “Do not touch the wires.”
opts: Let not the wires be touched.
The wires are not to touch.
Let not the wires being touched.
questions.why: Negative imperative passive: Let not + object + be + past participle. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: 'Sarkar Tumchya Dari' camps held across Goa during the Seva Sankalp Abhiyan 2026 aimed to:
opts: Register new voters for the 2027 polls
Distribute land titles under Mhaje Ghar
Bring government services and welfare schemes to citizens' doorsteps
Conduct free health check-ups for senior citizens
questions.why: Camps such as the one at Shiroda gave help with scheme applications. Sep 2026.

questions.q: Senior diplomat Sudhakar Dalela was appointed India's Ambassador to which country in October 2026?
questions.why: Dalela, a 1993-batch IFS officer, was India's BRICS Sherpa in 2026. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Who is named to take over as MD and CEO of HDFC Bank on 27 October 2026, succeeding Sashidhar Jagdishan?
questions.why: The RBI approved a three-year term for him. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Shubman Gill hit a record 117-ball ODI double century in September 2026 against which team?
questions.why: The innings came in the second ODI at Guwahati. Sep 2026.

questions.q: What was the theme of World Food Day 2026?
opts: Water is life, water is food
Hand in hand for better foods and a better future
Right to foods for a better life
questions.why: FAO's 2026 theme; the day marks FAO's founding on 16 October 1945. Oct 2026.

questions.q: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was shared by Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and:
questions.why: For discovering a molecular switch for nerve cells, the basis of optogenetics. Oct 2026.

questions.q: The fifth edition of India–Australia army exercise AUSTRAHIND began on 19 October 2026 at:
questions.why: It is held at the Foreign Training Node; a New Zealand observer team joined for the first time. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Police Commemoration Day, observed on 21 October, recalls the 1959 killing of ten policemen by Chinese troops at:
questions.why: Ten CRPF policemen died in the Hot Springs ambush on 21 October 1959. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Himachal Pradesh's first solar power project with a Battery Energy Storage System was inaugurated in October 2026 in:
questions.why: The 2 MW project with 1 MWh storage is at Rongtong in Lahaul and Spiti. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Vishvajit More made history in October 2026 by winning India's first silver in which style at the U-23 World Wrestling Championships?
questions.why: He won silver in the 55 kg category at Las Vegas. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Ravi is the sister of Sita. Sita is the father of Neha. How is Ravi related to Neha?
questions.why: Draw the family tree from the statements; the answer is Paternal aunt. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What comes next? JKL, MNO, PQR, STU, …
questions.why: Each group starts 3 letters after the last one, with the same pattern inside: VWX. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Statements: Some cats are dogs. No dogs are pets. Conclusions: I. Some cats are not pets. II. Some pets are cats.
questions.why: Checked against every possible diagram of the statements: I must be true, II need not be true. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What comes next? GHI, KLM, OPQ, STU, …
questions.why: Each group starts 4 letters after the last one, with the same pattern inside: WXY. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In a group of 70 people, 35 like tea, 24 like coffee and 27 like neither. How many like only tea?
questions.why: Both = 35 + 24 − (70 − 27) = 16; only tea = 35 − 16 = 19. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: The present ages of Neha and Kiran are in the ratio 2 : 6. After 4 years the ratio will be 5 : 11. What is Kiran's present age?
questions.why: Let the ages be 2k and 6k: (2k + 4)/(6k + 4) = 5/11 gives k = 3, so Kiran is 18. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In how many different ways can the letters of the word CANCER be arranged?
questions.why: 6 letters with repeats: 6! ÷ 2! = 360. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: If TABLET is written as UCEPJZ in a certain code, how is SYMPTOM written in that code?
questions.why: In the code the 1st letter moves 1 place, the 2nd 2 places, the 3rd 3 places, and so on: SYMPTOM → TAPTYUT. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In a group of 90 people, 52 like cricket, 30 like football and 21 like neither. How many like only cricket?
questions.why: Both = 52 + 30 − (90 − 21) = 13; only cricket = 52 − 13 = 39. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What comes next in the series? 5, 2, 7, 9, 16, …
questions.why: Each term is the sum of the two before it. Next: 25. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Long before Hahnemann, the idea that disease may be cured by similars was mentioned by:
questions.why: Hippocrates recognised both contraries and similars as ways of cure; Galen built his system on contraries.

questions.q: In 'The Genius of Homoeopathy', Stuart Close defined susceptibility as:
opts: the tendency of a disease to spread in a community
the power of a drug to produce symptoms in the healthy
the general quality of the living organism of receiving impressions, the power to react to stimuli
the strength of the medicine after potentisation
questions.why: Close: susceptibility is the capability of the living organism to receive impressions and react to stimuli; it governs both cure and the choice of dose.

questions.q: According to §27, the curative power of medicines depends on their symptoms being:
opts: opposite to the disease and equal in strength
similar to the disease but weaker than it
identical to the disease in every respect
similar to the disease but stronger than it
questions.why: §27: the curative power of medicines depends on symptoms similar to the disease but superior to it in strength.

questions.q: Psorinum is prepared from:
opts: the contents of the scabies (itch) vesicle
questions.why: Psorinum is the nosode of the itch vesicle; Syphilinum comes from the chancre.

questions.q: A sense of insecurity in the rectum, with stool escaping when passing flatus and lumps of jelly-like mucus, is characteristic of:
questions.why: Aloe: insecurity of the rectum, stool passes with flatus, jelly-like mucous lumps (Allen's Keynotes, Boericke).

questions.q: Inability to pass urine in the presence of others is characteristic of:
questions.why: Natrum mur (Allen's Keynotes): cannot pass urine in the presence of others.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a nosode?
questions.why: Pepsinum comes from the healthy stomach of an animal, so it is a sarcode; the others come from disease products.

questions.q: On a prescription, the 'subscription' gives:
opts: the patient's name, age and address
directions to the patient on how to take it
directions to the pharmacist on how to prepare or dispense the medicine
the name and potency of the medicine
questions.why: The subscription instructs the dispenser; directions to the patient form the signatura.

questions.q: In repertory language, 'opisthotonos' means:
opts: bending of the body to one side
spasmodic arching of the body backwards
spasmodic bending of the body forwards
questions.why: Opisthotonos is backward arching; forward bending is emprosthotonos and sideways bending pleurothotonos.

questions.q: Repertories such as Kent's, the TPB and BBCR, in which symptoms are reshaped to fit a fixed plan, belong to the:
questions.why: These repertories follow a logical plan built on a philosophy, unlike the Puritan works that keep the provers' words.

questions.q: The normal glomerular filtration rate in an adult is about:
questions.why: GFR is about 125 mL/min (180 L/day); 650 mL/min is about the renal plasma flow and 1.2 L/min the renal blood flow.

questions.q: Renin is secreted by the:
opts: cells of the proximal convoluted tubule
juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole
questions.why: The juxtaglomerular (granular) cells secrete renin; the macula densa senses tubular NaCl and signals them.

questions.q: Low serum albumin with a prolonged prothrombin time not corrected by vitamin K indicates:
opts: Impaired synthetic function of the liver
questions.why: Albumin and clotting factors are made by hepatocytes; failure of both, unresponsive to vitamin K, indicates loss of liver cell mass, as in cirrhosis.

questions.q: In liver function tests, an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2 suggests:
questions.why: Alcohol causes pyridoxal phosphate deficiency and mitochondrial damage, so AST rises more than ALT; viral hepatitis usually shows ALT above AST.

questions.q: Which of the following is used to treat an acute attack of gout?
questions.why: NSAIDs such as indomethacin, colchicine or corticosteroids treat the acute attack; allopurinol, febuxostat and probenecid are urate-lowering drugs for long-term control.

questions.q: The antiepileptic drug most strongly associated with neural tube defects when used in pregnancy is:
questions.why: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk, including spina bifida, and is avoided in women of childbearing potential where possible.

questions.q: The second booster of DPT vaccine under the UIP is given at:
questions.why: DPT booster-1 is at 16–24 months and booster-2 at 5–6 years; Td follows at 10 and 16 years.

questions.q: Constant nausea in pregnancy not relieved by vomiting, with a clean tongue, calls for:
questions.why: Persistent nausea unrelieved by vomiting with a clean tongue is the keynote of Ipecac; Nux and Ant crud have coated tongues.

questions.q: Under the UIP, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) is given as:
opts: three primary doses at 6, 10 and 14 weeks with no booster
one dose at birth and a booster at 9 months
one dose at 9 months and a booster at 16–24 months
two primary doses at 6 and 14 weeks and a booster at 9 months
questions.why: India uses a 2+1 PCV schedule: 6 weeks, 14 weeks and a booster at 9–12 months.

questions.q: The normal range of intraocular pressure is about:
questions.why: Normal IOP is 10–21 mm Hg; persistent values above this raise suspicion of glaucoma.

questions.q: Curling's ulcer is an acute stress ulcer of the stomach or duodenum seen after:
questions.why: Curling's ulcer follows major burns; Cushing's ulcer follows head injury or raised intracranial pressure.

questions.q: Called the 'homoeopathic knife' for its power to hasten suppuration in whitlow and abscess, the remedy is:
questions.why: Myristica sebifera hastens suppuration and is often said to shorten the course of panaritium.

questions.q: A net reproduction rate (NRR) of 1 means that:
opts: each woman bears exactly one child
the population is doubling every generation
each generation of mothers is exactly replaced by an equal number of daughters
the birth rate equals 1 per 1,000 population
questions.why: NRR = 1 is replacement-level fertility, roughly equal to a TFR of about 2.1.

questions.q: According to the Organon, the complete symptom picture of a prevailing epidemic disease (for the genus epidemicus) is obtained by:
opts: studying the first patient only, as he shows the purest symptoms
consulting the remedy used in the previous epidemic of the same name
noting only the pathological diagnosis common to all patients
careful observation of several cases, since each patient shows only part of the whole picture
questions.why: Organon §§100-102: each epidemic is treated as new, and the totality is gathered from several cases, as one patient presents only a portion of it.

questions.q: In a cohort study, the incidence of lung cancer among smokers minus that among non-smokers gives the:
questions.why: Attributable risk is the difference in incidence between exposed and non-exposed; it shows how much disease could be prevented by removing the exposure. Relative risk is the ratio.
